newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan lawmakers adopt nonbinding oil price freeze.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan lawmakers adopt nonbinding oil price freeze.

text.p: A panel of Taiwan's parliament adopted a non-binding resolution on Monday barring state monopoly Chinese Petroleum Corp from raising local oil prices before March 1.

Legislative Yuan economics subcommittee lawmakers who approved the resolution cited the likely inflationary impact of a petrol price on Taiwan's sluggish economic recovery and the likelihood it would boost the relatively high jobless rate.
Chinese Petroleum last week petitioned the Economics Ministry for permission to raise local petrol prices, but has declined to disclose how great of an increase it wanted.
Local media qouted monopoly sources as saying Chinese Petroleum was seeking increases of up to 10 percent. The company is prohibited to adjust prices by more than three percent in any one month.
It was not known if the resolution had wider legislative support or if parliament would further delay Chinese Petroleum's fiscal 1996-97 budget, which is already five months late.

There has been no indication whether the ministry would allow the requested increase, which has fuelled inflationary fears in Taiwan at time when economic recovery is coming more slowly than state and private forecasts had suggested.
The economics ministry was expected to form a committee to review price-hike proposal, with an emphasis on the inflationary impact, ministry officials have said.
Chinese Petroleum is eager to raise rates to overcome operating shortfalls blamed for November's pre-tax loss of T$1.129 billion (US$41 million).
The company had budgeted for a pre-tax profit of T$1.438 billion in the period and has blamed the sharp reversal on higher-than-expected world oil prices.

Government and private economists have said a 10 percent rise in petrol prices would cause the consumer price index to jump by about 0.43 percent in the month when it takes effect while the wholesale price index would jump 0.53 percent.
Taiwan consumer prices rose a year-on-year 3.19 percent in November, while wholesale prices actually fell an annual 3.02 percent, continuing a downward trend seen in recent months.
Chinese Petroleum's 95-octane petrol now sells for T$16.7 per litre (US$2.29 per gallon) at filling stations, including a T$0.2 per litre air-pollution surcharge.
Chinese Petroleum reported a cumulative budget deficit of T$8.126 billion for the July-November period.
Chinese Petroleum's November oil import costs averaged US$22.13 per barrel, much higher than the budgeted US$15.26 per barrel, according to figures disclosed by the company.
The oil monopoly imported 12.8 million barrels in November, bringing the cumulative total since the July 1 fiscal year start to 91.7 million barrels, the figures showed.
Taiwan, almost totally dependent on foreign crude, imports more than 150 million barrels a year.
